newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-LIFE AFTER SHEARER PROVES BLEAK FOR BLACKBURN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-LIFE AFTER SHEARER PROVES BLEAK FOR BLACKBURN.

text.p: How many players do you need to make up a football team? The answer -- if the team is Blackburn Rovers -- appears to be one.
Since Alan Shearer walked out on the 1995 English champions in July to join Newcastle United as the globe's most expensive player, Blackburn's world has fallen about their heads.
Every attempt to find a replacement for the England striker has failed and the 112 league goals he scored for them in four glorious seasons at Ewood Park are now just painful memories.
Ten matches into the season, the team which 17 months ago soared to the pinacle of English soccer are now the only side in the 92-team English Football League without a league win.
Rovers are anchored to the bottom of the premier league they once conquered and have just six league goals to their credit -- the same number Shearer has scored for Newcastle.
Blackburn's grandly titled "director of football" Kenny Dalglish has departed and manager Ray Harford, who joined the club with Dalglish in 1991, has considered following suit.

"Sometimes you think it might be better for everyone," he acknowledged gloomily after Rovers lost 2-0 at home to Arsenal earlier this month. "We're bottom of the league, haven't won a game, that's the situation."
On Tuesday things went from bad to worse as Blackburn were dumped out of the English League Cup at Ewood Park by second division Stockport, a team 34 places below them in the league.
At the final whistle, sections of the home crowd chanted for Harford to quit and around 150 fans staged a protest outside the ground to demand a new manager.
But for some fans at the north Lancashire club, Shearer, and not Harford, is the man at fault.

"I don't blame Harford at all," said Paul Loftus, editor of a Blackburn supporters' magazine. "Genuine Blackburn fans don't blame Harford. Not the fans who supported the club when we were down in the third division."
"The timing of Shearer's move has been our biggest problem," he said. "We had no time to find a replacement for him."
"If he'd left at the end of last season (rather than in late July) we could have found another number nine. He showed us no loyalty whatsoever."

"Losing him was not just like losing a striker. We lost a player who can play on the wings, who can cross the ball, who can drop back into midfield or defend. It was like losing three players in one."
Finding a substitute for Shearer has proved a tall order.
Harford tried to tempt Argentine striker Gabriel Batistuta from Italy's Fiorentina but the bid failed.
French internationals Christophe Dugarry and Zinedine Zidane were also said to be on Rovers' August shopping list but they went to Italy instead.
More recently the club has been linked with Brazilian goalscorer Bebeto but Blackburn insist he is not a target.

It is all a far cry from the heady days of the early 1990s when Blackburn, fuelled by the hard cash of local businessman and multi-millionaire Jack Walker, knew what they wanted and had the money to buy it.

Dalglish, manager at the time, broke the British transfer record twice in two years to buy Shearer for 3.3 million pounds ($5.3 million) in 1992 and fellow striker Chris Sutton for five million pounds ($8 million) in 1994.
Their goals brought the league title to Rovers and the club firmly believed it had established itself among England's elite.

"AC Milan were successful, so they had the money to spend, so they remained successful," a confident and relaxed Harford said at the time of Sutton's signing. "There's no reason why we shouldn't do the same."
Last season saw Blackburn start shakily and then rally in the New Year to finish seventh but, even then, the unity that won them the championship appeared to be on the wane.
Dalglish "moved upstairs", allowing Harford to become manager, and took a back-seat role at the club whose dreams he had helped fulfil.

"The best-paid golfer in English soccer" was how one British newspaper described the Scotsman, whose sporting priorities lay increasingly on the greens of northwest England rather than with the blue-and-whites of Ewood Park.
Dalglish left the club completely in August this year and since then Harford has been under ever-increasing pressure to start the Blackburn ball rolling again.
Few seriously believe they will be relegated and the manager still has the Shearer millions to spend on a substitute for England's European championship hero.
But if Rovers do not start scoring goals, Harford could soon be leaving Ewood Park with a former Blackburn terrace chant ringing in his ears: "There's only one Alan Shearer".
